The Canary rockfish (Sebastes pinniger) is a commercially important rockfish species inhabiting continental shelf and upper slope waters from the Gulf of Alaska to Baja California. This species exhibits a substantial ultimate body size, with the largest individuals reaching approximately 76 centimeters [Li = approximately 76 centimeters] in total length. The relationship between total length and wet body mass follows a length-weight power function with a scaling exponent near 3.09, indicating isometric growth. Using this relationship, the maximum recorded adult wet body mass for this species is estimated at approximately 6,500 grams [Wwi = approximately 6,500 grams]. Such large body sizes are typical of the subgenus Sebastosomus, which comprises several long-lived, slow-growing rockfishes. The energetic demands of achieving this size are considerable, particularly given the relatively low productivity of the species' preferred cold-water habitat. Field surveys have consistently documented individuals exceeding 70 cm, though the largest specimens are most commonly captured in deeper waters where fishing pressure is reduced. The length-weight relationship used to estimate these masses was derived from extensive sampling across the species' range and shows minimal geographic variation.

Sexual maturation in Canary rockfish occurs at a total length substantially smaller than the ultimate size attained by adults. Puberty is reached at approximately 44 centimeters [Lp = approximately 44 centimeters] in total length, a milestone that corresponds with a wet body mass of roughly 1,200 grams [Wwp = roughly 1,200 grams] based on the same length-weight regression. This size at maturity represents slightly more than half the maximum total length, a pattern common among iteroparous rockfishes that allocate considerable energy to somatic growth before initiating reproductive investment. The onset of gonadal activity in this species is closely tied to water temperature; females in warmer regions tend to mature at slightly smaller sizes, though the effect is modest across the species' latitudinal range. Histological examination of ovarian tissue reveals that vitellogenesis begins once females surpass this size threshold, generally between ages five and eight years depending on local environmental conditions. Males mature at a marginally smaller size than females, though the difference is not statistically significant in most populations studied.

Reproductive output in Canary rockfish is characterized by an exceptionally high fecundity, a common trait among live-bearing scorpaenids that release large numbers of planktonic larvae. At the thermal conditions typical of their habitat (5.9 °C [T = 5.9 °C]), females produce approximately 1,900,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,900,000 eggs per spawning event], with approximately 1 spawning event per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 spawning event per year]. This per-event fecundity represents an enormous annual investment in offspring production. The energetics of such high reproductive output impose considerable metabolic costs on gravid females. In comparison with other Sebastes species of similar body size, Canary rockfish exhibits an intermediate fecundity, lower than the highly fecund shortraker rockfish but substantially higher than the low-fecundity copper rockfish. This daily reproductive rate is achieved through a combination of high batch fecundity and protracted spawning duration rather than frequent spawning events.

The initial wet body mass at the earliest life stage is remarkably small, reflecting the viviparous reproductive mode of this species. Based on egg diameter measurements, the calculated mass of a newly fertilized ovum is approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams], derived from the spherical volume formula using a diameter of 0.8 millimeters. This minute mass is characteristic of pelagic-spawning rockfishes that produce large numbers of small, yolk-poor eggs. The larvae emerge from the maternal brood chamber at a similarly small size, having received no post-ovulatory nutrient supplementation beyond the initial yolk provisions. The transition from endogenous to exogenous feeding occurs rapidly after parturition, as the yolk reserves are quickly exhausted. This tiny starting mass contrasts sharply with the asymptotic adult body mass of 6,500 grams [Wwi = 6,500 grams], representing a mass increase of more than seven orders of magnitude over the lifespan. Such extreme growth potential necessitates a prolonged period of juvenile development.

Maximum lifespan in Canary rockfish is considerable, with the oldest documented individuals living for approximately 30,660 days [am = approximately 30,660 days] under the cold-water conditions typical of this species, specifically at 5.9 °C [T = 5.9 °C]. This longevity places the species among the longer-lived members of the genus Sebastes, though it does not approach the extreme lifespans exceeding 200 years recorded for some deep-dwelling rockfishes. The estimated maximum lifespan of 84 years is based on otolith increment analysis from individuals captured in long-term fishery-independent surveys. The slow growth and late maturity characteristic of this species are consistent with the life-history strategy of a long-lived, iteroparous predator occupying a relatively stable environment. The combination of pronounced longevity and a modest annual reproductive output per day results in a lifetime fecundity that is high, but distributed across many breeding seasons. Intraspecific variation in longevity is linked to depth gradients, with individuals inhabiting deeper, colder waters exhibiting slower somatic growth rates and correspondingly longer lifespans than conspecifics from shallower, warmer areas.
